We present excellent resolution and high sensitivity Very Large Array (VLA) observations of the 21cm HI line emission from the face-on galaxy NGC 1058, providing the first reliable study of the HI profile shapes throughout the entire disk of an external galaxy. Our observations show an intriguing picture of the interstellar medium; throughout this galaxy velocity-- dispersions range between 4 to 15 km/sec but are not correlated with star formation, stars or the gaseous spiral arms. The velocity dispersions decrease with radius, but this global trend has a large scatter as there are several isolated, resolved regions of high dispersion. The decline of star light with radius is much steeper than that of the velocity dispersions or that of the energy in the gas motions.

outputs.L1: We present high-resolution, high-sensitivity Very Large Array (VLA) observations of 21 cm H I line emission from the face-on galaxy NGC 1058, providing the first reliable study of H I profile shapes across the entire disk of an external galaxy. Our observations reveal an intriguing picture of the interstellar medium: throughout the galaxy, velocity dispersions range from 4 to 15 km s⁻¹ but show no correlation with star formation, stars, or the gaseous spiral arms. Although the velocity dispersions decrease with radius, this global trend exhibits considerable scatter, with several isolated, spatially resolved regions of high dispersion. The radial decline in starlight is much steeper than that of either the velocity dispersions or the energy associated with gas motions.
outputs.L2: Using high-resolution, highly sensitive Very Large Array (VLA) measurements of 21 cm H I emission, we have conducted the first dependable analysis of H I line-profile shapes across the full disk of the face-on galaxy NGC 1058. The data reveal a complex interstellar medium: velocity dispersions span 4–15 km s⁻¹ across the galaxy, yet show no relationship to star formation, the stellar distribution, or the gaseous spiral structure. Although dispersion generally declines toward larger galactic radii, substantial scatter surrounds this trend because several distinct, spatially resolved regions exhibit unusually high values. Moreover, stellar light falls off with radius far more rapidly than either the velocity dispersion or the energy associated with gas motions.
outputs.L3:
High-resolution, high-sensitivity Very Large Array (VLA) observations of the 21 cm H I emission from NGC 1058 provide the first reliable opportunity to examine neutral-hydrogen line-profile shapes across the full disk of an external galaxy. The measured H I velocity dispersions range from approximately 4 to 15 km s⁻¹. These dispersions show no clear correlation with regions of active star formation, the stellar distribution, or gaseous spiral arms, suggesting that the observed gas motions are not governed solely by these structures.

Although the velocity dispersion generally decreases with increasing galactocentric radius, the relationship exhibits considerable scatter. Much of this scatter is produced by isolated, spatially resolved regions with unusually high velocity dispersions. Moreover, the galaxy’s starlight declines with radius far more rapidly than either the H I velocity dispersion or the kinetic energy associated with gas motions. Thus, significant neutral-gas motions persist even in the faint outer disk, where the stellar contribution is comparatively weak.
outputs.L4:
High-resolution, high-sensitivity Very Large Array observations of the 21-cm H I line were used to examine the distribution and kinematics of neutral atomic hydrogen across the nearly face-on disk of NGC 1058. The galaxy’s favorable orientation minimizes line-of-sight contamination from large-scale rotation, allowing the shapes and widths of the H I emission profiles to provide a relatively direct measure of local gas motions. Maps of the line profiles and velocity dispersions reveal considerable spatial variation throughout the disk.

The measured H I velocity dispersions range from approximately 4 to 15 km s⁻¹. Although the dispersion generally decreases with increasing galactocentric radius, the decline is gradual and is superimposed on numerous localized regions of enhanced line width. These enhancements do not show a consistent spatial relationship with sites of recent star formation, the stellar distribution, or the gaseous spiral structure. Consequently, stellar feedback alone is unlikely to account for all of the observed motions.

A comparison with the galaxy’s light distribution further shows that the kinetic energy associated with the neutral gas declines much more slowly with radius than the stellar surface brightness. Significant gas motions therefore persist even in the faint outer disk, where the density of stars and the level of star-formation activity are low. The observations suggest that additional mechanisms—such as gravitational instabilities, magnetically driven turbulence, or energy supplied by continuing gas accretion—may help maintain the H I velocity dispersion across NGC 1058.

# The Very Large Array

The Very Large Array (VLA) is one of the world’s most powerful radio astronomy observatories. Located on the Plains of San Agustin in New Mexico, the facility consists of 27 large radio antennas, each measuring 25 meters in diameter. Together, these antennas operate as a single enormous telescope.

The antennas are positioned along three railway tracks arranged in a Y shape. By moving them closer together or farther apart, astronomers can change the resolution and field of view of the array. At its widest configuration, the Very Large Array spans approximately 36 kilometers.

Unlike optical telescopes, the VLA detects radio waves emitted by objects in space. This allows scientists to study distant galaxies, black holes, pulsars, supernova remnants, and regions where new stars are forming. Radio astronomy can also reveal objects hidden behind clouds of cosmic dust that block visible light.

Since beginning operations in 1980, the Very Large Array has contributed to many important discoveries. It has helped researchers examine the center of the Milky Way, investigate powerful cosmic explosions, and search for evidence of planets forming around young stars. Its distinctive antennas have also appeared in films and television programs, making the observatory a recognizable symbol of astronomical research.

The Very Large Array demonstrates how multiple instruments can work together to explore the universe with remarkable sensitivity and precision.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract summarizing high-resolution VLA observations of 21 cm H I emission in the face-on galaxy NGC 1058, emphasizing velocity-dispersion patterns and their relationship to star formation and galactic radius.
counterfactuals.output: We present high spatial- and spectral-resolution VLA observations of the 21 cm H I emission in the nearly face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1058. The favorable orientation permits a direct examination of line-of-sight velocity dispersion with minimal contamination from rotational broadening. The H I profiles reveal a structured dispersion field: elevated dispersions occur preferentially in the inner, star-forming disk and are often associated with regions of recent massive-star formation, although the correspondence is not one-to-one. Azimuthally averaged, the dispersion declines with galactocentric radius, from roughly 10–12 km s⁻¹ near the center to about 6 km s⁻¹ around and beyond the optical radius. Significantly, a finite and comparatively uniform H I dispersion persists in the extended outer disk, where tracers of active star formation are weak or absent. These results indicate that stellar feedback likely contributes substantially to turbulent motions within the optical disk, while additional processes—such as thermal broadening, magnetorotational instabilities, accretion, or other large-scale dynamical mechanisms—are required to maintain the observed velocity widths at large radii.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the main findings of a radio astronomy study examining H I profile shapes across the entire disk of NGC 1058.
counterfactuals.output:
Because NGC 1058 is almost face-on, rotational broadening is small, so its 21-cm spectra closely trace local atomic-gas motions. The study found that:

- H I profiles throughout the disk are generally not well represented by a single Gaussian.
- Most show a narrow central core plus broader, low-level wings, often modeled as two components: a cold/quiescent component with a dispersion of a few km s⁻¹ and a warmer or more turbulent component with a dispersion of roughly 8–10 km s⁻¹.
- Line widths and component strengths vary across the galaxy and generally decrease outward, but broad H I persists beyond the bright, star-forming optical disk.
- Local profile asymmetries and unusually broad lines are associated with organized motions such as shells, expanding structures, or other noncircular flows.
- Since significant broadening remains where star formation is weak, stellar feedback alone cannot maintain all the observed H I turbulence; additional processes such as gravitational stirring, accretion, or magnetorotational instabilities are likely involved.

Overall, the profiles indicate a multiphase, dynamically structured atomic interstellar medium rather than a single uniform H I population.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise research-paper abstract about the interstellar medium of NGC 1058 based on sensitive VLA measurements, including the observed 4–15 km/s velocity dispersions.
counterfactuals.output: We present sensitive Very Large Array H I observations of the nearly face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1058, tracing the distribution and kinematics of its neutral interstellar medium. The measured line-of-sight velocity dispersions span approximately 4–15 km s⁻¹ and vary significantly across the disk, indicating that the atomic gas cannot be described by a single uniform turbulent width. Regions of enhanced dispersion are plausibly associated with recent star formation and stellar feedback, while the lowest values characterize dynamically quiescent gas. The persistence of substantial H I velocity widths beyond prominent star-forming regions suggests that additional processes, including gravitational instabilities and large-scale gas motions, may help maintain turbulence. These observations constrain the energy balance, vertical support, and phase structure of the interstellar medium in low-density spiral disks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how neutral hydrogen velocity dispersion varies across NGC 1058 and whether it correlates with stars, star formation, or gaseous spiral arms.
counterfactuals.output:
Across NGC 1058, the H I velocity dispersion generally declines with galactocentric radius: it is roughly 10–15 km s⁻¹ in the inner disk and falls to about 5–7 km s⁻¹ in the extended outer H I disk, where it remains measurable well beyond the optical edge.

The spatial variations do **not** closely follow the stellar light, H II regions or other star-formation tracers, nor do enhanced dispersions consistently trace the gaseous spiral arms. Thus stellar feedback may contribute locally—especially in the inner disk—but it cannot by itself explain the widespread H I turbulence, particularly in the outer disk.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an astronomy abstract reporting that H I gas motions in NGC 1058 decline with radius more slowly than starlight and contain isolated regions of unusually high dispersion.
counterfactuals.output: We present an analysis of the neutral atomic hydrogen (H I) kinematics in the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 1058. Using spatially resolved 21-cm observations, we map the H I velocity field and velocity dispersion across the disk and compare their radial behavior with the stellar surface-brightness distribution. The characteristic amplitude of the gas motions declines with galactocentric radius substantially more slowly than the starlight, indicating that appreciable non-thermal H I motions persist well beyond the optically bright disk. In addition to this extended component, the dispersion map reveals several spatially isolated regions with unusually broad H I line profiles relative to their surroundings. These features are not part of a smooth radial trend and may trace localized energy injection, unresolved bulk flows, or disturbances associated with recent accretion. The results show that the outer H I disk of NGC 1058 remains dynamically active where the stellar contribution is weak, and that its kinematics cannot be described by a simple dispersion profile tied directly to the distribution of starlight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
